title: What Organs Help the Human Body Function?

opener.title: What Organs Help the Human Body Function?
opener.question: Your body has dozens of organs, each with its own job. How do they work together to keep one body alive?
opener.alt: An opening film that starts on Earth seen from space, then zooms to Florida, to a runner on a track, to a chest X-ray, to a heart, and finally to heart muscle cells under a microscope.

frames.label: Earth, from a million miles away
frames.line: More than eight billion people live on this planet.

frames.label: Florida, seen from space
frames.line: Right now, millions of them are walking, eating, sleeping, or running.

frames.label: A runner on a track
frames.line: Take one runner. Every step needs dozens of organs working at once.

frames.label: Inside the chest, on an X-ray
frames.line: An X-ray shows ribs, lungs full of air, and a heart in the middle.

frames.label: The heart (a model)
frames.scale: about the size of a fist
frames.line: The heart is a pump made of muscle. It never takes a day off.

frames.label: Heart muscle cells under a microscope
frames.scale: each cell less than 0.2 mm long
frames.line: Zoom in, and the heart is made of cells. Together they squeeze about 100,000 times a day.

k-warmup.text: This is a real X-ray of a person's chest. Where is the heart? Tap to drop your pin, or drag it. Then tap Save my pin and write why you put it there. You will check it in Part 4.

k-words.text: Organ. Function. Brain. Heart. Lungs. Skeleton.

k-part1.text: William Harvey printed this book in sixteen twenty-eight. Tap each yellow line to read it in plain English. Then try his famous test on Figure 2: slide the blood along the vein, and find out which way it can go.

k-quiz.text: Three quick questions, just for you. They are not graded. Tap an answer and read the note under it. Think about which organs work as a team.

k-assign.text: Now add your half of page nineteen. Answer the two Part B questions. In Part C, write your notebook page and use your reaction time. Then tap evidence cards in the planner to build your C-E-R about how your organs work together.

pin.title: Pin the heart
pin.intro: This is a real X-ray of a healthy adult's chest. Bones show up white. Air in the lungs looks dark. Where is the heart?
job: Tap the X-ray where you think the heart is.
Drag the pin to move it.
pin.alt: A black and white chest X-ray seen from the front. The spine runs down the middle, ribs curve around both sides, and the dark lungs fill most of the chest.
pin.credit: X-ray: Mikael Häggström (CC0), via Wikimedia Commons. An X-ray is shown as if the person is facing you, so their left side is on your right.
pin.notYet: Tap the X-ray to drop your pin.
pin.placed: 📍 Pin placed. Drag it, nudge it, or tap Save my pin.

zones.left: far over on the person's left side

pin.saved: 📍 Saved. You will check your pin in Part 4 of The Lesson.

wordlens.intro: Tap a word to see what it means.

words.def: A body part that does a specific job. The heart, lungs, brain, and stomach are all organs.
The job an organ does. The heart's function is to pump blood. The brain's function is to think and control the body.
The organ that controls everything else. Thinks, remembers, senses, and tells the body what to do.
The organ that pumps blood. Beats nonstop, sending oxygen and nutrients to every part of the body.
The pair of organs that pull in oxygen and push out carbon dioxide. Two of them, one on each side of the chest.
The frame of bones that supports the body, protects organs, and helps you move.

source.title: William Harvey's own words
source.alt: Two printed pages from William Harvey's 1628 book. The left page is Latin text with a fancy border and a large letter S. The right page shows two drawings of a man's arm gripping a stick, with a cloth band tied above the elbow.
source.intro: William Harvey was a doctor in London, England. He was also the doctor of King Charles I. For years he studied hearts in many animals. In 1628 he printed a short book in Latin, the language scientists used then. It showed that the heart pumps blood out to the body, and the blood comes back to the heart again, around and around.
job: Tap each yellow line to read it in plain English.
Then find the two lines in the hunts.

lines.en: To the most serene and unconquered Charles, King of Great Britain, France, and Ireland, Defender of the Faith.
Most serene King: the heart of animals is the foundation of their life, the chief of all their parts,
the sun of their little world. All growth depends on it, and all strength and energy flow out from it.
In the same way, a King is the foundation of his kingdom and the heart of his nation.
So I dare to offer Your Majesty what I have written here about the motion of the heart.
Figure 1. A band is tied around the upper arm. The veins swell up, and small knots appear along them. Harvey wrote that each knot is a valve, a tiny flap inside the vein.
Figure 2. A finger presses the vein and pushes the blood along, toward the heart, past a knot. Behind the finger, the vein stays empty. Nothing flows back, because the valve will not let it.

asks.q: Hunt 1: Find the line where Harvey calls the heart the “chief” of the body.
asks.yes: Yes. Harvey thought the heart was the boss. Keep that in mind for Part 2.
asks.no: Not that one. Look on the left page, just after the big letter S.

asks.q: Hunt 2: Find the figure where a finger pushes blood along a vein.
asks.yes: Yes. Figure 2. Now try it yourself, just below.
asks.no: Not quite. Look at the right page. Which arm has a finger pressing on it?

source.credit: Source: William Harvey, Exercitatio anatomica de motu cordis et sanguinis in animalibus (Frankfurt, 1628), page 3 and Figures 1 and 2. Scan of the 1628 pages from the 1928 facsimile edition (Internet Archive, public domain in the U.S.). Plain-English version written for this lesson; the figure lines follow Harvey's own explanation in Chapter 13.

vein.title: Slide the vein
vein.intro: This is Harvey's Figure 2, bigger. The band tied around the upper arm makes the arm veins swell with blood, so you can see them. The purple line shows the blood in one vein. The hand is at the top. The heart is the other way, past the band.
vein.alt: Harvey's Figure 2: a forearm with a fist at the top and a cloth band near the bottom. A finger presses on a vein near the letter H. The letters O and G mark spots further down the vein.
steps: Put your finger on the vein at the thumb spot and slide it DOWN, toward the heart, past the valve. Or tap the button.
Now lift the thumb. Watch the empty part of the vein.
Put your finger on the vein below the valve and slide it UP, toward the hand. Or tap the button.
vein.okDown: The blood slid right past the valve. The thumb blocks the vein, so the part behind your finger stays empty.
vein.okLift: The empty part filled up again, from the hand side. New blood was already coming from the hand.
vein.okUp: Stuck! The valve stops the blood, and the vein just bulges at the knot. The harder you push, the more it swells.
vein.hintDown: Start at the orange thumb spot and slide all the way past the yellow valve.
vein.hintUp: Start below the yellow valve and slide up until you reach it.
vein.missVein: Put your finger right on the purple vein.
vein.ask: So which way can blood move in the veins of your arm?

opts.hint: When you slid toward the hand, did the blood get past the valve?
Compare your two slides. Did both directions work?

vein.win: Only toward the heart. The valves are one-way doors. Veins carry blood back to the heart, and the heart pumps it out again. Harvey used tests like this to show that blood goes around in a circle.
vein.tryTitle: Try it on your own hand (optional)
vein.tryText: Let one hand hang down for 30 seconds until the veins on the back of it stand out. Press one vein with a fingertip. With another finger, slide along the vein toward your wrist, then lift that finger. Does the vein stay flat for a moment? Stop if anything feels uncomfortable.
vein.credit: Figure 2 from William Harvey, De motu cordis (1628), from the 1928 facsimile (Internet Archive, public domain in the U.S.). The purple vein, thumb, and valve marks are a model added for this game.

brain.name: Brain
brain.job: Thinks, feels, and sends messages to the body

eyes.name: Eyes
eyes.job: Sense organs: see light, shapes, and colors

heart.name: Heart
heart.job: Pumps blood to every part of the body

lungs.name: Lungs
lungs.job: Take in oxygen and push out carbon dioxide

stomach.name: Stomach
stomach.job: Mashes food and mixes it with juices

intestines.name: Intestines
intestines.job: Finish breaking down food and pass nutrients and water into the blood

liver.name: Liver
liver.job: Cleans the blood and makes bile that helps digest fat

pancreas.name: Pancreas
pancreas.job: Makes digestive juices and helps control sugar in the blood

kidneys.name: Kidneys
kidneys.job: Filter waste and extra water out of the blood

bladder.name: Bladder
bladder.job: Stores urine until you go to the bathroom

skin.name: Skin
skin.job: Keeps germs out, senses touch and heat, sweats to cool you

muscles.name: Muscles
muscles.job: Pull on bones to move you

skeleton.name: Skeleton
skeleton.job: Holds you up. The skull protects the brain; the ribs protect the heart and lungs

knock.kicker: Part 2 game · Watch the model fail
knock.title: Knock one out
knock.intro: Harvey called the heart the chief. But can any organ work alone? Switch one organ off and see what happens to the rest of the team.
job: Tap an organ to switch it off.
Predict: how soon is the body in trouble?
Watch who fails next. Test the heart, lungs, and stomach.
knock.start: Tap an organ above to switch it off.
knock.predictQ: If the {o} stops, how soon is the body in trouble?
knock.notQuite: Not quite. The body is in trouble {s}. Watch the chain to see why.
knock.notTested: The {o} matters too, but today, test the heart, the lungs, and the stomach. Tap the {o} again to switch it back on.
knock.backOn: The {o} is back on. Pick another organ.

chain.t: The heart stops pumping. Blood stops moving.
The lungs still fill with air, but no blood comes by to pick up the oxygen.
The brain can't store oxygen. With no blood flowing in, a person faints in about ten seconds.
The muscles run out of oxygen too and stop working.

cases.end: Within seconds. That is why doctors rush to restart a heart.

chain.t: The lungs stop. No new oxygen gets into the blood.
The heart keeps pumping, but the blood it sends out has less and less oxygen.
After a few minutes without oxygen, brain cells start to be harmed.
Muscles weaken. Even the heart muscle needs oxygen to keep going.
Food is not broken down, so fewer nutrients get into the blood.
Slowly, the muscles have less fuel to use.
The brain runs low on energy too, so it is hard to think.

cases.end: Only after days. Your body stores some energy, so it can wait longer for food than for oxygen.

knock.win: Every organ needs the others. The brain needs the heart, the heart needs the lungs, and they all need food from the stomach. They just fail at different speeds: no blood in seconds, no oxygen in minutes, no food in days.
knock.whyTitle: Why does the brain feel it first?
knock.why: Your brain is only about 2% of your body weight, but it uses about one fifth of the oxygen you breathe in. It can't store oxygen, so it needs fresh blood all the time.
knock.credit: Organ pictures: Servier Medical Art, Laboratoires Servier (CC BY-SA 3.0), via Wikimedia Commons. These are drawn models of real organs.

reflex.title: Race the reflex
reflex.intro: When you touch a hot pan, your hand jumps back. Is that your brain deciding to move? First, measure how fast you can react on purpose.
job: Wait. The moment the pan glows red, tap it as fast as you can.
reflex.alt: A small frying pan sitting on a portable gas camping stove, outdoors on grass and dirt.
reflex.msgIdle: Tap Start, then wait for red.
reflex.msgEarly: Too soon! Wait for the red glow. Tap Start to try again.
reflex.msgGot: {t}! Tap the button for your next try.
reflex.note: Your eyes saw the red, your brain decided, and then it told your finger muscles to tap. That takes time. A reflex skips the deciding.
reflex.wow: Your hand starts pulling away from a hot pan BEFORE your brain feels the heat. The message takes a shortcut through your spinal cord.
path: Skin senses the heat and sends a message up a nerve.
The spinal cord, inside your backbone, sends a message straight back to the arm muscles.
The muscles pull your hand away.
A moment later, the brain gets the message and you feel “Ouch, hot!”
reflex.credit: Photo: Itai, “Portable gas stove and frying pan” (public domain), via Wikimedia Commons. Screen times are rough: your device adds a little delay.

team.intro: Organs almost never work alone. For each moment below, light up every organ that is doing a big part of the work.
team.more: Your body has many more organs than these, more than 70 in all. One more kind is reproductive organs. They make it possible for adults to have children.
team.title: Who is on the team?
job: Tap organs to light them up. Tap again to turn one off.
Tap Check my team. Finish all four moments.
team.missHint: Someone is missing from the team.

cases.title: A: You run up two flights of stairs.
cases.text: Your chest feels tight and your heart pounds.

hint.muscles: What actually lifts your legs up each step?
hint.lungs: Where does the extra oxygen come in?
hint.heart: What sends the oxygen to your legs?
hint.brain: What tells your legs when to move?

wrong.stomach: Your stomach isn't doing the climbing. During hard exercise, digestion actually slows down.
wrong.bladder: The bladder isn't helping you climb.

cases.win: Lungs bring in oxygen, the heart pumps it to your leg muscles, the brain runs the moves, and your skeleton gives the muscles something to pull on.

cases.title: B: You eat a sandwich at lunch.
cases.text: By recess, you have energy to play.

hint.stomach: Where does the sandwich get mashed and mixed with juices?
hint.intestines: Where do the nutrients pass into the blood?
hint.heart: How do the nutrients travel from your belly to your legs?

wrong.bladder: The bladder stores urine. It doesn't digest food.
wrong.lungs: The lungs handle air, not food.

cases.win: The stomach mashes the food, the pancreas and liver add juices, the intestines pass the nutrients into your blood, and the heart pumps them to your muscles.

cases.title: C: You touch a hot pan.
cases.text: You yank your hand back before you even think.

hint.skin: What senses the heat in the first place?
hint.muscles: What actually pulls your hand back?
hint.brain: Remember Part 3. Who feels “Ouch!” a moment later?

wrong.stomach: The stomach has nothing to do with this one.
wrong.kidneys: The kidneys aren't part of this quick move.

cases.win: Skin senses the heat, the spinal cord sends a quick message to the muscles, the muscles pull your hand back, and then the brain feels the burn.

cases.title: D: You drink a big glass of water.
cases.text: Later, you need to go to the bathroom.

hint.intestines: Where does the water pass into your blood?
hint.heart: How does the water in your blood reach other organs?
hint.kidneys: What filters the extra water out of your blood?
hint.bladder: Where does the urine wait until you go?

wrong.lungs: The lungs handle air, not the water you drink.
wrong.skeleton: Your bones aren't part of this job.

cases.win: The intestines pass the water into your blood, the heart pumps the blood to the kidneys, the kidneys filter out the extra water as urine, and the bladder stores it.

team.compareTitle: Prediction vs. evidence: where is the heart?
rows: Did it land on the heart?
team.evWhere: Near the middle of the chest, tipped a little to the person's left (your right on the X-ray). The big white shape in the middle is the heart.
team.evShape: The heart sits between the two lungs, right behind the breastbone, with the ribs around it like a cage.

twist.head: Lots of people think the heart is on the far left of the chest.
twist.line: But the heart sits near the middle, tucked between the lungs. Only its bottom tip leans to the left, and that is where you feel the strongest beat.
twist.chain: Look at your four teams. No moment used only one organ. Even Harvey's “chief” can't do its job without the lungs, the blood, and the brain.

How do body systems team up?

planner.title: Plan before you write
planner.intro: Tap two or more pieces of evidence to add them to your Evidence box. Then write your claim and reasoning in your own words.
cards: When the heart stopped, the brain was in trouble within seconds, because no blood brought it oxygen.
When the lungs stopped, the heart kept pumping, but the blood had no fresh oxygen, so the brain was harmed within minutes.
Running up the stairs needed the lungs, heart, muscles, and brain all at once.
A sandwich needs the stomach and intestines to break it down and the heart to send the nutrients to the muscles.
My hand pulls off a hot pan before my brain feels the heat: the skin, spinal cord, and muscles work together.
In Harvey's test, blood in a vein moved only toward the heart.

checklist: Warm-Up: your heart pin and two sentences of reasons.
Part B: questions 1 and 2, in complete sentences.
Part C: your notebook page (both boxes).
C-E-R: a claim, at least two examples of organs working together, and your reasoning.

footage.title: A heart cell beating all by itself
footage.intro: Scientists in Japan grew this single human heart muscle cell from stem cells in a lab dish. It is alone, with no brain and no body attached.
look: Watch the cell squeeze and relax, over and over.
Nothing is telling it to beat. Heart muscle can start its own beat.
Count how many squeezes you see in the clip.
footage.credit: Video: Uosaki H. and others (2011), PLOS ONE 6(8): e23657, Movie S2 (CC BY 2.5), via Wikimedia Commons. Enlarged and muted for this lesson.

data.title: Heartbeats per minute, from mouse to elephant
data.unit: beats per minute at rest (the middle of the normal range)
data.intro: Animal doctors and heart doctors measure resting heartbeats. Here is the middle of the normal range for seven mammals, from smallest to biggest.
job: Drag across the bars to read each number.
Look at how the bars change as the animals get bigger.
data.ask: What pattern do you see in the data?

opts.hint: Read the mouse bar, then the elephant bar. Which one is taller?

opts.t: Every animal's heart beats about the same
opts.hint: Compare 600 for the mouse with 30 for the elephant. Are they close?

data.win: Bigger animals have slower heartbeats. A mouse's heart beats about 600 times a minute, an elephant's about 30. A blue whale's heart can slow to about 2 beats a minute on a deep dive.
data.alt: A bar graph of resting heartbeats per minute: mouse 600, hamster 450, rabbit 265, cat 130, adult human 80, horse 34, elephant 30.
data.credit: Data: Merck Veterinary Manual, “Resting Heart Rates” table (mouse 450–750, hamster 300–600, rabbit 180–350, cat 120–140, horse 28–40, elephant 25–35); American Heart Association, normal adult resting rate 60–100. Bars show the middle of each range. Blue whale: Goldbogen and others (2019), PNAS 116: 25329.

cabinet.title: A heart-rhythm monitor from 1969
cabinet.alt: A 3D scan of a wooden console with a white front panel covered in rows of buttons, switches, and small lights, with cables coming out the back.
cabinet.text: This is a real prototype from the Smithsonian. Dr. L. Julian Haywood, an African American heart doctor, set up a special heart-care unit at Los Angeles County General Hospital in 1966. In 1969 his team built this console. Working with a computer, it watched the beats of heart-attack patients and helped catch beats that went wrong. It worked because every heartbeat makes its own tiny electric signal.
cabinet.credit: 3D model: Prototype of a digital heart rhythm monitor developed by Dr. L. Julian Haywood, National Museum of African American History and Culture, Smithsonian. CC0.
